x_to_y: This edge represents the idea that changes in \(x\) cause changes in \(y\), i.e., \(x\) is a policy/treatment/input that directly shifts the outcome \(y\). The main threats are omitted confounders that affect both \(x\) and \(y\), reverse causality if \(y\) also feeds back into \(x\), and selection or measurement error that makes \(x\) correlated with unobserved determinants of \(y\). Next, the researcher should articulate and justify an identification strategy (e.g., random assignment, IV, DiD, RD) and then assess balance/pre-trends/placebos and sensitivity to alternative controls/specifications to probe remaining confounding.
y_to_z: This edge represents a causal effect of \(y\) on \(z\): changing \(y\) is assumed to directly shift \(z\) through some economic mechanism (e.g., policy intensity affecting outcomes, prices affecting quantities, or investment affecting productivity). The main risk is that the estimated effect is not causal because \(y\) is endogenous—unobserved factors may jointly affect \(y\) and \(z\), \(z\) may also feed back into \(y\) (reverse causality), or \(y\) may be measured with error leading to attenuation or bias. Next, the researcher should articulate and test plausible identifying variation in \(y\) (e.g., an instrument, policy discontinuity, or credible timing), check balance and pre-trends if using quasi-experimental designs, and probe robustness to alternative controls or specifications that would block major backdoor paths in the DAG.
